chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar from Mu'awiya ibn Hakim from Ibn Abi Umayr from Jamil from a man from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Regarding

A man who had a slave, and the slave was taken into the House of Polytheism (Dar al-Shirk), then was taken as captive to the House of Islam. He (Abu Abdillah) said: 'If he was taken possession of by the master before division (of spoils), he is for him; and if division was carried out regarding him, he is more entitled to the price.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: The compiler of this book issues fatwa based on what the first two reports contained, that his property is returned to the Muslim if evidence is established for him, as long as he has not been divided; and whenever he is divided, it is not obligatory to return him to him except with the price, but he is given his value from the treasury. And this is so that it does not lead to the annulment of the division. As for not returning him to him and not giving his value, it is not permissible in any case, because with the polytheist's seizing him, he did not acquire ownership of him until it becomes valid for him to be considered Fay' (spoils). It is also permissible to say that he is returned to him in all cases, and the buyer returns to the Imam with the price of that. Indicating this is what was narrated:
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a Muslim slave captured by polytheists and later reclaimed?
ai.summary: This ruling from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* addresses the specific fiqh of *Fay'* (booty) regarding the reclamation of slaves captured by polytheists, distinguishing between pre-division possession (*qabla al-qism*) and post-division compensation (*ba'd al-qism*). Al-Tusi highlights the juristic debate on whether the polytheist's hold is merely provisional or if it solidifies ownership, ensuring that the original Muslim owner is never left without recourse, either through restitution or monetary valuation from the *Bayt al-Mal*. This reflects the Shia emphasis on preserving property rights during the transitional state of war and conquest.
